title: Bisulfid vs Bisulfide: Meanings, IUPAC Names and German Usage
summary: The two words look like one term in two spellings. The cited sources do not treat them that way: an English dictionary defines bisulfide as disulfide, a chemical database lists bisulfide as a synonym for the hydrosulfide ion, and the German dictionaries consulted record Sulfid but not Bisulfid.
reference_task: What do bisulfide (English) and Bisulfid (German) mean according to authoritative sources, which chemical species is each word attached to, and how do they relate to sulfide, disulfide and bisulfite?

at_a_glance.label: bisulfide in a chemical database
at_a_glance.value: listed as a synonym of {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.molecular_formula}} (PubChem CID {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.cid}})

at_a_glance.label: German Bisulfid
at_a_glance.value: not in the DWDS contemporary lexical sources

modules.heading: English bisulfide: the dictionary sense is disulfide

paragraphs.text: Merriam-Webster enters {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFIDE:lexical.headword}} as a {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFIDE:lexical.part_of_speech}} whose whole definition is a cross-reference: “{{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFIDE:lexical.definition_quoted}}”. The dictionary dates its first known use to {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFIDE:lexical.first_known_use}}.
Read with the disulfide entry below, the dictionary sense of bisulfide is a compound with two sulfur atoms. The entry gives no sense that involves hydrogen.

modules.heading: Bisulfide as a database synonym for HS⁻

paragraphs.text: PubChem record CID {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.cid}} has the formula {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.molecular_formula}}, the computed IUPAC name {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.computed_iupac_name}} and the title {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.record_title}}, and its synonym list includes “{{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.synonym_listed}}”.

The same English spelling therefore points to two different species in two kinds of source: the dictionary maps it to disulfide, two sulfur atoms, while the database attaches it to the hydrosulfide ion, one sulfur and one hydrogen. A synonym list records names that are in use; it is not a naming recommendation.

The IUPAC 2005 recommendations on inorganic nomenclature give the anion {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.anion}} two names: {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.substitutive_name}} as the substitutive name and {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.additive_name}} as the additive name ({{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.section}}).
Bisulfide is not one of the names given in that example. Where precision matters, the IUPAC names identify HS⁻ without the ambiguity of the bi- form.

Merriam-Webster gives {{EVD-TERM-MW-DISULFIDE:lexical.headword}} two senses: “{{EVD-TERM-MW-DISULFIDE:lexical.sense_1_quoted}}” and “{{EVD-TERM-MW-DISULFIDE:lexical.sense_2_quoted}}”, with a first known use of {{EVD-TERM-MW-DISULFIDE:lexical.first_known_use}}.

For the anion {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-S2-NAMES:lexical.anion}} the same recommendations give {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-S2-NAMES:lexical.homopolyatomic_name}}, and {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-S2-NAMES:lexical.parent_hydride_name}} on the parent-hydride basis ({{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-S2-NAMES:lexical.section}}).

Merriam-Webster defines {{EVD-TERM-MW-SULFIDE:lexical.headword}} in two senses: “{{EVD-TERM-MW-SULFIDE:lexical.sense_1_quoted}}”, and “{{EVD-TERM-MW-SULFIDE:lexical.sense_2_quoted}}”. Its first known use is {{EVD-TERM-MW-SULFIDE:lexical.first_known_use}}.
Merriam-Webster defines {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFITE:lexical.headword}} as “{{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFITE:lexical.definition_quoted}}”, first known use {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFITE:lexical.first_known_use}}.
Bisulfite is one letter away from bisulfide, but the dictionary defines it through sulfite, not sulfide. The two words should not be used interchangeably.

For {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.anion}} IUPAC accepts the abbreviated name {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.accepted_abbreviated_name}}; the full hydrogen name is {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.full_hydrogen_name}} ({{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.section}}). IUPAC adds: “{{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.list_status_quoted}}”.

PubChem record CID {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-BISULFITE:lexical.cid}}, titled {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-BISULFITE:lexical.record_title}}, has the formula {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-BISULFITE:lexical.molecular_formula}} and the computed IUPAC name {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-BISULFITE:lexical.computed_iupac_name}}.
The database therefore places bisulfite on an oxygen-containing anion, not on any sulfide.

Duden defines {{EVD-TERM-DUDEN-SULFID:lexical.headword}} as “{{EVD-TERM-DUDEN-SULFID:lexical.definition_quoted}}”. The DWDS entry (source: {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-SULFID:lexical.dictionary}}) labels the word {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-SULFID:lexical.domain_label}} and defines it as “{{EVD-TERM-DWDS-SULFID:lexical.definition_quoted}}”.
Both German definitions, a salt of hydrogen sulfide, match the second English sense of sulfide given above. For this pair the spellings differ and the meaning is the same.

In its entry {{EVD-TERM-SPEKTRUM-HYDROGENSULFIDE:lexical.entry}}, the Spektrum chemistry lexicon states that hydrogen sulfide forms two series of salts: {{EVD-TERM-SPEKTRUM-HYDROGENSULFIDE:lexical.salt_series}}.
In this German reference work the salts of HS⁻ are called Hydrogensulfide. The passage does not use the word Bisulfid.

modules.heading: German Bisulfid is not in the dictionary

paragraphs.text: For {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-BISULFID:lexical.headword}} the DWDS answers: “{{EVD-TERM-DWDS-BISULFID:lexical.coverage_statement_quoted}}” It shows {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-BISULFID:lexical.forms_shown}}.
The DWDS gives the same answer for {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-HYDROGENSULFID:lexical.headword}}: “{{EVD-TERM-DWDS-HYDROGENSULFID:lexical.coverage_statement_quoted}}”
Missing from a dictionary is not the same as never used. It means that general German lexicography does not record the word, so a German dictionary cannot settle what Bisulfid refers to.

modules.heading: Why German writes -id where English writes -ide

paragraphs.text: A German university teaching text on inorganic nomenclature states the rule: “{{EVD-TERM-FHM-ID-RULE:lexical.rule_quoted}}” Its table of monatomic anions lists the sulfide ion as “{{EVD-TERM-FHM-ID-RULE:lexical.example_row}}”.
The rule explains the spelling Sulfid. It does not say what Bisulfid refers to, and none of the dictionaries or nomenclature sources cited here defines Bisulfid.

not_established.heading: What this reference does not establish
not_established.text: BISULFID is the name of this website. The name is not a chemical claim, and this reference does not state that German Bisulfid is the equivalent of English bisulfide. Some German industry pages use Bisulfid for HS⁻, and one was captured verbatim, but an industry page is not an admissible source for terminology here, so that usage is recorded as a boundary and not adopted. The IUPAC Gold Book entry on hydrosulfides could not be retrieved openly when the sources were captured, and a second German teaching handout was unreachable, so neither is cited. The history of the bi- prefix, how often each spelling is used, and the safety or industrial properties of any species named here are outside this reference [SOURCE REQUIRED].
